rationale: AC-3.22 specifies exit code 3 for a run with conflicts, while N-000608 specifies exit 5 for a run where checking is incomplete. Both describe exit codes for different run states, but if a single run has both conflicts and incomplete checking, the exit codes cannot both apply.
note: Different run states: AC-3.22's exit 3 is for a completed run with conflicts; N-608's exit 5 is for checking stopped incomplete by the call cap. pipeline.py checks 'incomplete' before 'open_conflicts' -- one run can't be both.

rationale: AC-3.22 specifies a run with two conflicts produces output with an exit code of 3 (implying the run completes and reports the conflicts); N-000288 requires 'the run never stops at a conflict', which contradicts reporting conflicts as the outcome.
note: N-288 ('the run never stops at a conflict') is why AC-3.22's scenario is reachable at all -- the two agree, they don't compete.

rationale: AC-3.22 states the report includes 'the item' (attention item) in a run with one attention item; N-000296 states conflicts are not attention items, but both claims involve the same run context, and AC-3.22's inclusion of an attention item contradicts N-000296's constraint if a conflict were treated as one.
note: AC-3.22's 'the item' is the one attention item its own Given clause sets up, not the conflicts. N-296 is not disputed by either claim.

rationale: Claim A requires the run to end with a complete report of all processed items; Claim B states that an unexpected exception discards the run and its records, preventing the normal report generation that Claim A mandates.
note: Different run outcomes: N-291 describes a normally-completing run's report; N-398 (F3 D35) describes an unhandled exception that discards the run before any report is written.

rationale: AC-6.16 states that when a re-judgement answers `none`, `conflict_ids` are cleared and the record is resolved. N-000197 states that a conflict record resolved by deletion keeps its members. These describe conflicting outcomes for what happens to conflict record data upon resolution.
note: Different fields: AC-6.16 clears the node's conflict_ids; N-197 (F2 D14) is about the record's members list. Neither claim touches the other's field.

rationale: N-000291 requires that the report include 'every conflict found', while N-000296 states 'Conflicts are not attention items'. Since N-000291 specifies conflicts must be in the report and N-000296 specifies they are not attention items, there is an apparent contradiction about what the report should contain regarding conflicts.
note: Conflicts and attention items are two separate categories listed in one report sentence (N-291); N-296 saying conflicts aren't attention items doesn't stop both being listed.

rationale: A states facts stay in their own fields; B requires recomputing derived fields at layer C, which moves field values across the system (derived_field implies computed values that leave original fields).
note: Two halves of one rule (F2 status.6): facts (e.g. conflict_ids) stay stored where they are; derived fields (status, related_conflict_nodes, registry, meta counts -- N-437's own list) are recomputed from those facts. Not the same fields.

rationale: Claim A requires a conflict record below two members to be resolved and keep its member list; Claim B requires an open conflict record to never list a deleted node, which precludes keeping member history that includes deleted nodes.
note: N-199 explicitly scopes itself to 'an open record'; N-198 is about a record already resolved by deletion -- F2 D14 states both, contrasting open vs resolved on purpose.

rationale: Claim A requires attention list items to be added to the review queue; Claim B states that conflicts are NOT attention items. If conflicts are what would be added per Claim A, but Claim B excludes them from being attention items at all, these cannot both hold for the same entity.
note: Different subjects: N-245 is about a block that failed atomization twice; nothing in it or N-296 links that path to conflicts.

rationale: AC-5.15 requires that exhaustive mode "judges nothing"; N-000623 states "A conflict closes only on re-judgement or member deletion". If exhaustive mode produces no judgments, it cannot close conflicts via re-judgement, creating a logical conflict about whether exhaustive mode's results can affect conflict state.
note: Exhaustive mode (sddc pairs --exhaustive) never judges pairs at all -- it simply isn't one of the ways N-623 says a conflict can close.

rationale: AC-3.22 requires exit code `3` when a run has two conflicts and one attention item; AC-3.5 requires exit code `5` when max_calls_per_run is exceeded. Both specify exit codes for the same run, and a run cannot simultaneously exit with both codes.
note: Different Given clauses: AC-3.22 assumes the run completed; AC-3.5 assumes max_calls_per_run was reached first. One run hits at most one precondition.

rationale: Both claims specify exit codes for the same run, but AC-3.22 states exit code is `3` while N-000808 states exit code is `5`—these cannot both hold for the same run at the same time.
note: Same class as CF-000017 -- the call cap (N-808) and a completed run with conflicts (AC-3.22) are different run outcomes, not simultaneous.

rationale: AC-3.22 requires a run with conflicts to exit with code 3; AC-6.11 requires a run with no conflicts to exit with code 0. Both cannot hold simultaneously for the same run's exit code when conflicts are present or absent.
note: AC-6.11's own Given is 'a graph with no conflicts' -- the literal opposite precondition of AC-3.22's. Mutually exclusive by construction.

rationale: AC-3.22 specifies exit code 3 for a run with conflicts; AC-6.12 specifies exit code 5 for a constrained run. Both define the exit code for their respective scenarios, and the codes cannot be both 3 and 5 for the same run.
note: When checking is incomplete (AC-6.12's precondition) the conflict count isn't final yet, so exit 5 takes precedence over exit 3 in the code's own ordering -- a precedence rule, not a contradiction.

rationale: AC-6.17 states when a member is deleted, the record is resolved and marked as such; N-000197 states a resolved record keeps its members, which contradicts the implication that deletion removes members.
note: Complementary: AC-6.17 sets the resolution reason (member_deleted) when a member is deleted; N-197 says what happens to the members list when that happens (kept, not cleared).

rationale: N-000437 requires recomputing derived fields; N-000527 requires they never be edited—these cannot both hold for the same derived fields at the same time.
note: 'Recompute' (N-437) via the write-transaction derivation step is the only way a derived field is ever set; N-527's 'never edited' means no other code path touches it directly. Same rule.

rationale: A says a conflict record resolved by deletion keeps its members; B says an open conflict record never lists a deleted node. Since deletion creates deleted nodes, a record that 'keeps its members' after deletion contradicts the requirement that open records 'never list a deleted node' when those members include deleted nodes.
note: Same as CF-000067 -- N-199 is scoped to open records; N-197 describes one already resolved.

rationale: AC-6.11 states that when a graph has no conflicts, the run exits 0; N-000608 states the run exits 5 when checking is incomplete. Both refer to the same run's exit behavior for different graph states, and these exit codes cannot occur simultaneously for the same run state.
note: Different run states -- a clean pass (AC-6.11) and a cap-stopped incomplete check (N-608) can't both describe the same finished run.

rationale: A requires a graph with no conflicts while B requires the same graph to hold open conflicts; both cannot be true for the same graph at the same time.
note: AC-6.11 and N-328 are explicitly the no-conflicts and has-conflicts branches of one check phase, never both true of one graph at once.

rationale: N-000197 states a conflict record keeps its members when resolved by deletion, while N-000695 states the record must be closed (resolved) with reason `member_deleted` when a member is deleted; these describe conflicting outcomes for the same event (member deletion).
note: N-197 and N-695 state the same closure rule (F2 D14 and F6 sec4.6) in two places -- closer to a mistyped duplicate than a contradiction.

rationale: AC-6.10 specifies the report exits 3 when conflicts exist; AC-6.11 specifies the report exits 0 when there are no conflicts. These describe mutually exclusive exit codes for the same report in different conditions but represent contradictory outcomes for the same operation.
note: Same mutually-exclusive precondition pair as CF-000140 (conflicts present vs AC-6.11's explicit 'no conflicts').

rationale: Claim A states the registry no longer lists resolved conflicts, while Claim B indicates conflicts remain readable via the conflicts view file, which is identified as a kind of registry.
note: N-751 never calls the conflicts view 'a registry' -- that identification is the judge's own inference. The registry (conflicted_nodes.json) and the conflicts view (views/conflicts.md) are different files, and both only ever list open records anyway.

rationale: Both claims specify mutually exclusive conditions for the same node_status field: one requires `stale_reasons` to be non-empty (status=stale), the other requires `last_checked_run` to be null (status=unchecked). A node cannot simultaneously be in both stale and unchecked states.
note: Two rows of the same status-precedence table (F2 status derivation), not simultaneous claims about one node; AC-2.12's precedence order resolves any overlap.

rationale: Claims specify mutually exclusive node_status values: stale (with non-empty stale_reasons) versus validated (none of the above conditions). A single node cannot simultaneously have status=stale and status=validated.
note: 'None of the above' (N-134) is definitionally the last rule in the same table N-132 belongs to -- it can't fire when N-132's condition already did.

rationale: Claim A states that attention_list_items must be listed at the end of the run; Claim B explicitly states that conflicts are NOT attention items. If conflicts are not attention items but must appear in the report, these claims establish different categories at the same endpoint.
note: Same non-overlap as CF-000279/CF-000243/CF-000166 -- attention items and conflicts are separate report categories.

rationale: When conflict_ids and ambiguity are both non-empty, A requires status to be `conflict`; when stale_reasons is non-empty, B requires status to be `stale`. These cannot both hold if all three conditions are simultaneously present.
note: AC-2.12 is the acceptance criterion that proves the precedence table (N-132 is one row of it) holds for every combination of facts -- it settles N-132, it doesn't compete with it.

rationale: Claim A requires deleting links when a node is deleted, but Claim B requires all links to have existing `from` and `to` nodes at the same time—both cannot hold if a node deletion leaves orphaned links before they are cleaned up.
note: N-185's link deletion happens in the same transaction as the node deletion; N-443's consistency check runs on the committed graph (F4 sec4.2), never on a mid-transaction state.

rationale: Claim A specifies deletion removes node records and links entirely; Claim B specifies editing replaces fields and adds stale_reasons to links. A node cannot be both deleted and edited in the same transaction.
note: Different alignment outcomes for a block (F3 sec4.6): N-180 is the 'source text gone' delete path; N-273 is the 'source text changed' edit path -- never both for one block.

rationale: Claim A requires the node record be deleted, while Claim B requires the same node record to have its fields replaced, which are mutually exclusive operations.
note: Same class as CF-000027 -- delete and edit are mutually exclusive alignment outcomes for a block, not two requirements on one record.

rationale: AC-6.10 specifies the run exits 3 when conflicts are found; AC-6.12 specifies the run exits 5 when a call cap is reached. Both cannot occur in the same invocation since they define mutually exclusive exit codes for different scenarios.
note: Same precedence as CF-000141 -- an incomplete check (AC-6.12) is decided before the conflict count (AC-6.10) is even final.

rationale: Both specify mutually exclusive node_status values: unchecked (when last_checked_run is null) versus validated (none of the above). A node's status cannot be both unchecked and validated simultaneously.
note: Same table-row pattern as CF-000159: N-134 ('none of the above') can't fire when N-133's unchecked condition (last_checked_run null) already did. Rows of one precedence table, not simultaneous claims.

rationale: Claim A states node records remain untouched except source.lines; Claim B states fields are replaced. Both address what happens to the same node record and cannot both hold for the same editing scenario.
note: N-272 (unchanged) and N-273 (edited) are adjacent rows of F3's alignment-outcome table (align.py: unchanged/edited/split/new/merged/removed) -- different, mutually exclusive outcomes for one block, not simultaneous requirements.

rationale: A states the run never stops at a conflict; B states the run stops with exit 5 when a per-run cap is reached—both apply to the same run and cannot both hold.
note: Same source sentence as CF-000024 -- 'never stops at a conflict' (check phase) vs the call cap (N-808) stopping the run. Different triggers; verified against the actual F3 sec4.8 text.

rationale: A requires deletion of a node's record when its source text is gone; B requires that an unchanged node keep its whole record except its source—these directly contradict when both refer to the same node at the same time.
note: Same class as CF-000161/168 -- delete (N-180, source text gone) and unchanged (N-820, D22) are mutually exclusive alignment outcomes.

rationale: AC-5.15 states exhaustive mode makes no judgments ('judges nothing'), while N-000545 states the check phase makes one judgment per pair, creating a direct conflict about whether judgments occur.
note: Exhaustive mode (AC-5.15) makes no model calls at all -- it is not one of the paths N-545's 'one judgement per pair' describes (which is about the normal check phase's cost, per D13's source text). Different commands.

rationale: AC-2.13 states a freshly placed node with null last_checked_run has status 'unchecked, never validated'; N-000134 defines 'validated' status as occurring when 'none of the above' (other conditions are false). A freshly placed node matches 'none of the above' conditions, creating a contradiction.
note: Traced through derive_status's actual precedence: a freshly placed node (last_checked_run null) satisfies N-133's `unchecked` condition, which is checked BEFORE `validated`('none of the above', N-134) is ever reached. AC-2.13 and N-134 do not even share an overlapping precondition.

rationale: AC-5.15 requires that exhaustive mode "judges nothing, and makes no model call"; N-000604 states that "Pair judging and atomization share `atomizer.max_calls_per_run`". If exhaustive mode makes no judgments, it cannot participate in pair judging and thus cannot share a model-call budget with atomization.
note: Same non sequitur as CF-000232 -- exhaustive mode makes no calls, so it can't violate a shared-budget rule (N-604) that only applies to things that call the model.

rationale: A requires link endpoints exist as nodes (among other options); B states deleted nodes no longer exist and appear in no index. A deleted node cannot simultaneously be a valid link endpoint and not exist.
note: Same as CF-000019 (already judged) -- N-185's deletion cascade removes every link touching a deleted node in the same transaction; N-443's endpoint-existence check runs on the committed graph (F4 sec4.2), so no dangling link is ever externally observable.

rationale: AC-3.5 states the run exits 5 when max_calls is reached with pending blocks remaining, while N-000290 states the run continues to the last pending block. Both cannot be true simultaneously.
note: N-288/N-290 are one sentence in F3 sec4.8 ('The run never stops at a conflict... the run continues to the last pending block') about the check phase not stopping when a conflict is found. AC-3.5 is about the call-cap budget being exhausted -- a different stopping condition entirely; checked the source, they are not even about the same trigger.

rationale: Claim A requires the node record be deleted; Claim B states it remains untouched except for `source.lines`—both cannot hold for the same deletion event.
note: Delete (N-143, F2 sec4.9: source text gone) and unchanged (N-272, F3's alignment table: same text) are mutually exclusive block outcomes -- a block is aligned to exactly one.

rationale: A states a pair is judged again when its text changes, implying multiple judgments for the same pair; B asserts the check phase makes one judgment per pair, which cannot coexist for the same pair in the same scope.
note: N-545 is D13's rationale for max_pairs_per_node ('the check phase makes one judgement per pair' -- within one run, explaining why fewer candidate pairs means fewer calls). AC-6.14 is about a pair being judged again in a LATER run after a text change. Checked N-545's source: it's about cost per run, not a lifetime-once rule.

rationale: AC-3.22 specifies the report must name conflicts, blocks, and nodes and exit 3; AC-6.10 specifies the report must name conflicts with details and exit 3. AC-3.22's broader requirement (naming blocks and nodes processed) already encompasses the report naming conflicts.
note: AC-3.22 (F3's compile-level report) and AC-6.10 (F6's conflict-section detail) are complementary descriptions of one report from two governing specs, not competing.

rationale: AC-3.22 specifies what a report contains (conflicts, items, blocks, nodes, model usage) and the exit code, which encompasses N-000612's requirement that output emits content as one object.
note: AC-3.22 is about report CONTENT; N-612 is about the --json FORMAT (one object) for scripting. Different aspects of the same report, not competing.

rationale: AC-6.16 describes what happens when a re-judgement answers `none` (record is resolved, conflict_ids cleared). N-000199 is a constraint that an open conflict record must never list a deleted node. AC-6.16's resolution scenario already implies the constraint in N-000199.
note: Different scenarios (re-judged-to-none vs. deletion) loosely linked by the judge; neither implies the other, but there's no actual tension either.

rationale: Claim A requires that runs report every node formed; Claim B states that deleted nodes do not appear in indexes. Since deleted nodes are a kind of node, Claim A's requirement to report all nodes formed implies Claim B's constraint about deleted nodes not appearing.
note: Spurious: 'nodes formed' this run (N-291) says nothing about deleted nodes from earlier (N-680) -- different populations.

rationale: Claim B states run_output includes 'the graph, a conflict report, and generated human views'; Claim A specifies a particular requirement (graph_hash) that must be carried by the graph component. B subsumes A because specifying the graph is output already implies A's requirement can be part of how the graph is included.
note: N-792 never mentions graph_hash; the judge's own rationale calls the link 'already implies A's requirement CAN be part of' -- speculative, not an actual implication. Spurious pairing via the shared `run_output` family, not a defect.

rationale: Claim B's description of how the `atomizer.max_calls_per_run` cap stops a run with exit code 5 is an instance of the shared behavior that Claim A states is used by both pair judging and atomization.
note: N-604 and N-808 are two specs (F6, F3) stating the same shared-cap fact -- consistent, not competing.

rationale: N-000138 states that `related_conflict_nodes` is computed from records and never written independently; N-000159's requirement that members list an id in `conflict_ids` while a record is open is an instance of how this computed field is maintained through record-based operations.
note: N-138 (related_conflict_nodes) and N-159 (conflict_ids on members) are about two different fields; the judge's link is vague and not substantiated. Spurious, not a defect.

rationale: Claim A states that a run continues to the last pending block; Claim B states that a resumed run continues predictably. Since resumed run is a kind of run, A's specific requirement about how runs continue to pending blocks already implies the more general claim that resumed runs continue predictably.
note: Different subjects: N-290 is about not stopping mid-run when a conflict is found; N-610 is about a separate, later run resuming predictably after an earlier stop. Linked only by the shared word 'continues'.

rationale: AC-1.10 specifies behavior when a list item is re-ingested (change tracking, id preservation); N-000610 only states that a resumed run continues predictably. AC-1.10's requirement of predictable, tracked changes subsumes the more general assertion.
note: Spurious: AC-1.10 (block-id tracking on edit) and N-610 (a resumed run continuing predictably) are about different subjects, linked only by loose vocabulary.

rationale: N-000437 specifies that the system must recompute derived fields including status and related_conflict_nodes, which subsumes AC-2.16's requirement that these fields be cleared and updated when a conflict is resolved.
note: AC-2.16 is a specific instance of N-437's general 'recompute derived fields' rule -- correct general/specific relationship, working as intended.

rationale: AC-2.12 defines the general status hierarchy rule; AC-6.16 describes the outcome when conflict records are resolved (status is re-derived), which is a specific application of AC-2.12's hierarchy without adding new constraints.
note: Same as CF-000136 -- AC-2.12 general, AC-6.16 a specific application of it.

rationale: A specifies the complete end-of-run report including conflicts and attention items; B states conflicts and attention items are reported at the end—A's detailed specification subsumes B's assertion.
note: N-291 lists the report's contents; N-335 (D4) states the never-stops-mid-run principle that is why the report waits until the end. Complementary.

rationale: N-000792 states the system outputs a graph and a conflict report; AC-6.11 specifies what happens when a graph has no conflicts. The output structure (N-000792) is presupposed by the conflict reporting behavior (AC-6.11).
note: N-792 is vision.md's brief output summary ('the graph, a conflict report, and generated human views'); AC-6.11 is a specific behavioural AC. General/specific, not a defect.

rationale: AC-6.16 specifies that when a contradiction is resolved, conflict_ids are cleared on both nodes and their status is re-derived. N-000131 defines the relationship between conflict status and non-empty conflict_ids. AC-6.16's action of clearing conflict_ids and re-deriving status already implies the status relationship N-000131 describes.
note: AC-6.16 clearing conflict_ids is consistent with N-131's rule (status=conflict when conflict_ids non-empty) -- once cleared, N-131's condition correctly no longer holds.

rationale: Claim B (recompute derived fields) subsumes Claim A (related_conflict_nodes is computed, never written independently) because recomputing derived fields necessarily means they are never written independently—the operation of recomputation enforces the constraint stated in A.
note: Same 'recompute is the only write path' pattern as CF-000051 -- N-138 and N-437 are complementary, not opposed.

rationale: B's requirement to recompute derived fields (including `status`) already implies A's specific rule for how the status field is derived from `atomized_hash`.
note: Name collision: N-57's 'status' is the F1 block classification (new/changed/unchanged, derived from atomized_hash); N-437's 'status' is the F2 node's conflict-derived status. Different fields sharing one English word.

rationale: B states a conflict closes only on re-judgement or member deletion; A is the specific case of deletion (one of B's two closure conditions). B's broader statement already implies A's narrower scenario.
note: N-197 (deletion keeps members) is a specific instance of one of N-623's (D4) two listed closure paths (member deletion). Correct general/specific relationship.

rationale: Claim A requires the run output to include a conflict report (among many things); Claim B states that output is 'a conflict report and generated human views.' Claim A's detailed requirement already implies Claim B's simpler statement about what run output contains.
note: Same class as CF-000199/215 -- N-792 (vision) and N-291 (spec detail) are general/specific, not competing.

rationale: N-000199's constraint that open records never list deleted nodes is the enforcement mechanism that ensures N-000159's requirement that members list the conflict id while the record is open.
note: N-159 (membership bidirectionality) and N-199 (no dangling deleted members) are two different invariants about open records, not one implying the other, but not in tension either.

rationale: Claim B lists the complete set of run outputs including graph and conflict report; Claim A describes specific properties of two of those outputs, which is already encompassed by B's statement of what outputs exist.
note: Same class as CF-000199 -- N-792 (vision summary) and N-328 (specific behaviour) are general/specific, not competing.

rationale: AC-3.17 specifies that when a block's atom aligns to an existing node with a judged link, the link's other end gains a `stale_reasons` entry; this directly implies the condition in N-000132 that node status is `stale` when `stale_reasons` is non-empty. AC-3.17 creates the non-empty stale_reasons, which subsumes the stale status requirement.
note: AC-3.17 is the mechanism that produces the condition N-132's status rule then acts on -- correct cause/rule relationship, not a defect.

rationale: Claim B is a general requirement that all links must have valid `from` and `to` endpoints (including nodes); Claim A is a specific instance of this requirement applied to the `decides` link type connecting decision nodes to changed nodes.
note: General link-existence rule (N-443) and a specific link-type declaration (N-193, decision D7) -- correctly complementary, not a defect.

rationale: AC-2.12 establishes the hierarchy that status becomes non-conflict when `conflict_ids` are empty; AC-2.16 describes a specific instance of this rule when a conflict record resolves, making AC-2.12 the broader principle that subsumes the narrower scenario in AC-2.16.
note: AC-2.12 (general precedence) and AC-2.16 (specific: conflict resolved) -- correct general/specific relationship.

rationale: AC-3.14 states that a node exists with status `unchecked` and `last_checked_run` null; N-000133 defines the relationship between the `unchecked` status and null `last_checked_run`. AC-3.14's requirement already implies N-000133's definition.
note: AC-3.14 is a test scenario applying N-133's table rule -- correct, not a defect.

rationale: AC-2.16 requires that when a node's only conflict record is resolved, its status is no longer conflict, which directly implies it cannot be in conflicted_nodes.json (which per N-000446 contains only nodes with conflict status).
note: AC-2.16's status transition and N-446's registry invariant are consistent -- once status leaves `conflict`, the node correctly drops out of conflicted_nodes.json.

rationale: N-000180 describes the lifecycle behavior (deletion in transaction) that governs nodes' membership in conflict records, which N-000137 simply states as a node field containing.
note: N-137 defines what the conflict_ids field holds; N-180 describes cleanup on deletion. Two different facts about the same field, not opposed.

rationale: Claim A states nothing stops mid-run and every conflict/attention item is reported at the end; Claim B restates only the conflict-reporting requirement as part of the broader nothing-stops-mid-run principle, so A's statement encompasses B's narrower focus.
note: N-335 (F3 D4) and N-790 (vision) restate the same never-stops-mid-run principle from two documents -- complementary, not a defect.

rationale: AC-1.9 establishes the general principle that pre-existing blocks keep their ids and are classified based on changes (unchanged vs new). AC-1.10 is a specific case where one block changes, building on the general preservation rule that AC-1.9 establishes.
note: AC-1.9 (insertion) and AC-1.10 (single-word edit) are parallel, distinct example scenarios in the same AC sequence (AC-1.9..1.11), not one subsuming the other.

rationale: Both claim that members list the conflict record id in conflict_ids while the record is open. A states 'Every member lists this id in conflict_ids while the record is open'; B states 'Every open conflict record's members list it in conflict_ids'—these are the same bidirectional relationship stated once from each direction.
note: N-159 (F2) and N-445 (F4's check-list) state the identical MUST-level fact -- 'while a conflict record is open, every member lists it in conflict_ids' -- independently, with no cross-reference between them. A genuine (mild) restatement risk: if one is edited, the other could silently drift. Worth a one-line cross-reference rather than two independent statements.

rationale: Both claims state the same requirement for batch runs: that things (findings/conflicts/attention items) are not settled or stopped mid-run and must be reported at the end. They express the same constraint using different terminology.
note: Lower confidence than the others in this batch. N-293 (sec4.9, attention items specifically) and N-335 (D4's rationale, conflicts+items together) overlap substantially, but N-335 is framed as part of the 'why the run never stops' decision rationale recapping context, and it also covers conflicts, which N-293 does not. Worth a second look.

rationale: Both claims state the same bidirectional relationship: nodes list conflict record IDs in their conflict_ids field (A), and conflict records list their member nodes and are reciprocally listed in those nodes' conflict_ids (B). They express the same constraint from different perspectives.
note: N-137 is a passive field definition (modality: none -- 'what conflict_ids holds'); N-445 is a MUST-level consistency check (F4 sec4.3's bidirectionality check). Different document roles (glossary entry vs. enforced invariant), not the same statement twice.

rationale: Both claims state the same requirement: when a conflict record's member count falls below two (N-000198) or a member is deleted (N-000695), the record must be resolved/closed with reason `member_deleted`; they describe the same event from different angles.
note: Checked the source: N-695 (F6) explicitly cites '(F2 sec4.9)' rather than restating the <2-members threshold -- it's a summary that deliberately defers detail to F2's D14 (N-198), not an independent, driftable restatement.

rationale: AC-1.31 states blocks become pending and remain in atomization pipeline. N-000167 states blocks marked `unchanged` by ingest would 'silently never be atomized.' These outcomes cannot both hold for the same blocks at the same time.
note: N-000167 is D13's rationale for a bug AC-1.31's design already fixes (pending derived from atomized_hash); not a live requirement, no contradiction

rationale: Claim A requires old blocks be kept (never deleted), while Claim B states that unprocessed blocks would silently never be atomized—describing what happens when blocks are not properly processed, contradicting the requirement to keep and maintain old blocks.
note: Different operations on a block: N-036 is about the RECORD never being physically deleted (persistence); N-167 (D13's now-fixed bug) is about ATOMIZATION coverage. A block can be kept forever and also, before the fix, never get atomized -- that combination is exactly the bug D13 fixed, not a contradiction.

rationale: Claim A states that unprocessed blocks would be silently never atomized after run failures, while claim B requires pending blocks to be processed in reproducible order; both concern block processing in runs, and the first says blocks are never atomized while the second expects them to be processed.
note: N-286's ordering guarantee applies to blocks that get processed; N-167 (D13, now fixed) described a bug in blocks that were NOT processed due to a stale flag. Different populations.

rationale: A requires every node of a block carry a label (whether or not the id was adopted); B restricts the block to form exactly one node only when a human id is adopted. These cannot both hold: if a block forms multiple nodes (not adopting the id), A requires all of them carry the label, contradicting B's condition.
note: N-177 and N-807 are two halves of the same F2 D12 rule -- label is unconditional (N-177), id-adoption is conditional on one node (N-807). N-177's own wording ('whether or not the id was adopted') shows it already assumes N-807's conditionality.

rationale: AC-2.2 states no node record is produced under certain conditions (overlapping quotes), while N-000807 states a block must form exactly one node when adopting a human id—these describe mutually exclusive outcomes for a block's node production.
note: Same class as CF-000059/66 -- N-807 doesn't claim every block forms exactly one node, so AC-2.2's split-required/zero-node case doesn't meet its condition.

rationale: N-000358 requires that one chunk runs every model step (including Q-ATOM, Q-DESC, Q-TERM which are model steps), while N-000521 states F5 makes no model calls at all; if F5 contains chunks, these requirements cannot both hold.
note: N-358's 'every model step' list (Q-ATOM, Q-DESC, split re-ask, Q-TERM) names only atomization steps; F5 (retrieval) makes no calls at all and isn't part of that chunk's steps -- confirmed against the actual retrieval code, which has no model call anywhere.

rationale: Claim A states F5 makes no model calls; Claim B states a lock hit makes no model call, which is a narrower exception. If F5 never calls the model, the lock-hit exception is vacuous, suggesting the claims assume different contexts.
note: N-594's lock-hit exception is about F6's Q-PAIR judging (which normally does call the model); F5 never calls the model in the first place. Different components, not inconsistent.

rationale: Claim A states F5 makes no model calls; Claim B (check phase) requires reporting how many calls were used, presupposing model calls exist in the system F5 participates in.
note: F5 (retrieval, selects candidates) and 'the check phase' (F6, judges them) are explicitly different phases in this architecture -- N-605's call count is F6's, not F5's.

rationale: AC-3.20 requires every question to be asked even with lock hits, while N-000241 requires re-asking only once on failure; these are incompatible behaviors for the same question under the same conditions.
note: --no-replay (AC-3.20, cache bypass) and the on-failure retry (N-241) are two independent, orthogonal mechanisms -- a --no-replay run can still hit a guard failure and get one retry.

rationale: AC-3.20 states every question is asked even with lock hits, while N-000247 states only the failed block is re-asked alone once; these describe mutually exclusive re-asking behaviors.
note: Same as CF-000083 -- replay-bypass and failure-retry are different mechanisms, not competing rules.

rationale: AC-3.16 states that when a block yields atoms one of which fails twice, no nodes are written; N-000269 states a block still completes even yielding zero atoms. These conflict on whether node writing occurs in failed-atom scenarios.
note: Different triggers: AC-3.16 is an atom that was proposed and then failed validation twice; N-269 is a block where the model correctly proposed zero atoms because nothing was a claim. Success vs. failure, not the same case.

rationale: Claim A states unprocessed blocks would 'silently never be atomized,' while Claim B requires the system to re-ask that block, implying it will be processed again.
note: Different scenarios: N-247 is the normal within-run retry mechanism (works correctly); N-167 (D13, fixed) was specifically about the boundary BETWEEN runs. Not the same failure path.

rationale: Claim A (N-000035) requires that remaining new blocks receive a new id and `new` status. Claim B (N-000167) describes unprocessed blocks (which can include new blocks per the term relationships) being marked `unchanged` and never atomized after early run termination. A block cannot simultaneously be marked `new` (A) and `unchanged` (B) for the same ingestion state.
note: Different populations and different moments: N-035 is identity-matching at ingest (new text -> new id); N-167 (D13, fixed) was a later bug in pending-status computation for already-known blocks. Not the same scenario, and the bug is fixed.

rationale: Claim A states a failed block stays pending with no node created; Claim B states a block forms exactly one node when adopted. Both cannot hold for the same block at the same time.
note: N-807 (F2 D12) is conditional -- 'the human id is ADOPTED only when the block forms exactly one node' -- it never claims every block forms exactly one node. N-673's zero-node failure case doesn't trigger N-807's condition at all.

rationale: A states blocks with only definition/context/rationale sentences form nothing; B states blocks form exactly one node under certain conditions; these cannot both be true for the same block at the same time.
note: Same non-overlap as CF-000059 -- N-807 is about id-adoption, conditional on one-node blocks; N-391's zero-node blocks simply don't meet that condition.

rationale: A states F5 makes no model calls, while B states model access must use Claude Code with Haiku. If F5 must never make model calls, it cannot use Claude Code (which is a model-based tool).
note: Same class as CF-000043/72/85 -- N-736 specifies the model/backend for calls that happen; F5 is the one component that makes none.

rationale: AC-3.6 states a question is asked exactly twice when validation fails, while N-000247 states a failed validation re-asks only that block alone, once. These specify incompatible numbers of re-asks.
note: Not competing numbers: AC-3.6's 'asked exactly twice' (total) and N-247's 're-asks... once' (the re-ask count alone) describe the same fact -- 1 original ask + 1 re-ask = 2 total. Same figure, two framings.

rationale: Claim A requires pending blocks to be processed in `(source path, first line)` order for reproducibility; Claim B states they are processed in chunks of 20. Chunk-based processing contradicts deterministic source-path-first-line ordering required for reproducibility.
note: Chunking (N-357, batches of 20) is a batching layer on top of the ordering (N-286), not a replacement for it -- chunk 1 is the first 20 in order, chunk 2 the next 20, etc.

rationale: A states F1 makes no model calls, while B requires recording telemetry for model calls (backend, model, tokens); these cannot both be true for the same F1 component at the same time.
note: N-233's telemetry rule binds whichever component makes a call (F3, F6); it never claims F1 makes one. F1's zero calls and N-233's per-call rule don't overlap.

rationale: F1 MUST NOT make model calls, while model calls MUST go through one interface—these cannot both hold for the same system at the same time.
note: Same class as CF-000043 -- N-766 (constitution) binds calls that happen (by F3/F6); F1 making none doesn't conflict with a rule about how calls that DO happen are routed.

rationale: N-000008 forbids F1 from making model calls; N-000565 requires model calls to ask questions about pairs—they cannot both hold if F1 and the model-calling phase are part of the same system.
note: Same class as CF-000043/72 -- N-565 describes F6's Q-PAIR judging, a different component from F1.

rationale: N-000233 requires recording model calls with specific telemetry, while N-000594 explicitly states no model call is made when a lock hit occurs.
note: N-233's telemetry rule applies to calls that happen; N-594 says a lock hit makes no call, so there's nothing for N-233 to record -- consistent, not competing.

rationale: AC-3.20 with `--no-replay` flag states 'every question is asked even with lock hits' (bypassing replay); N-000283 states that a lock hit 'replays the stored answer' with conditional re-asking. These directly contradict what happens to questions when a lock hit occurs.
note: Different preconditions: AC-3.20 assumes --no-replay is set (bypasses the cache); N-283 describes the default, replay-enabled behaviour. Mutually exclusive flag states, not contradictory.

rationale: AC-3.16 states none of the three nodes is written (persisted) in a failure scenario, while N-000142 states a node is deleted when its source atom is gone—these describe incompatible outcomes for the same node at the same time.
note: Different moments: AC-3.16 is a first-time write failure (nothing was ever created); N-142 is deletion of a node that existed and whose source later vanished. Not the same event.

rationale: Claim A states all ingested blocks are pending when none are atomized; Claim B states fenced code blocks are not in the pending set when `include_code_blocks: false`. Both cannot hold for the same fenced code block under the same ingestion conditions.
note: Different populations: AC-1.31 covers three ordinary blocks; AC-1.6 is the explicit carve-out for fenced code blocks under a profile setting. Build-plan I-6 itself notes the code correctly distinguishes these.

rationale: AC-3.19 requires zero model calls during a recompile with no changes, while N-000358 requires every chunk to run all model steps before any is kept; these cannot both hold for the same recompile scenario.
note: AC-3.19's scenario has nothing pending (a pure replay), so the chunk loop in N-358 never executes at all -- N-358 describes what happens when a chunk runs, not a claim that one always must.

rationale: Claim A states that unprocessed blocks marked unchanged must not be silently atomized after early run termination, which subsumes the specific case in Claim B where a block fails checks twice and must stay pending (no node created). The pending state is the mechanism that prevents atomization.
note: Not really related: N-167 (D13, a now-fixed cross-run bug in the stale-flag) and N-673 (the correct, intended within-run retry-then-pending behaviour) are about two different things, not one subsuming the other. Spurious pairing, not a defect.

rationale: AC-3.18 describes a specific deletion scenario (when a block is removed), which is one of the cases covered by the general rule in N-000142 about when nodes are deleted.
note: AC-3.18's 'removed block' scenario is one of N-142's two listed deletion triggers -- correct general rule / specific acceptance criterion, not a defect.

rationale: AC-3.18 describes the full deletion scenario including the stale_reasons consequence, which subsumes the specific requirement in N-000186 about neighbors gaining stale_reasons entries.
note: AC-3.18 is the testable acceptance criterion instantiating the same stale_reasons rule N-186 (D3) states generally -- correct AC-restates-decision structure.

rationale: AC-3.18 states that neighbours with judged links gain stale_reasons entries; N-000146 restates this same requirement more narrowly—AC-3.18 covers the full scenario while N-000146 covers just one part of it.
note: Same AC-restates-decision structure as CF-000009 -- AC-3.18 is the full acceptance criterion, N-146 an earlier, narrower decision-list item.

rationale: B subsumes A by specifying that removed nodes and their links are deleted with transactional atomicity and conflict record cleanup, which encompasses A's requirement that nodes and links are deleted when a block is removed.
note: AC-3.18 is a testable instance of N-181's (D3) general 'removed nodes are deleted' decision -- correct general/specific.

rationale: AC-3.18 states that when a block is removed, neighbours gain stale_reasons entries. N-000655 states that nodes lose stale reasons during check phase. AC-3.18's creation of stale_reasons (as a consequence of deletion) implies the existence and later removal described in N-000655.
note: Two halves of one lifecycle, not one subsuming the other: staleness is CREATED by AC-3.18's deletion event, then CLEARED later by N-655's check-phase event. Sequential, not simultaneous.

rationale: AC-6.6 describes a complete behavior: re-ask once, and on failure no verdict is recorded. N-000241 only requires re-asking once. AC-6.6 subsumes N-000241 because it specifies the re-asking requirement plus additional consequences.
note: N-241's re-ask-once rule lives in F3's shared batch mechanism (atomize/batch.py's ask_each), used by every question kind including Q-PAIR -- AC-6.6 is F6's own acceptance criterion for that same shared rule, not a competing one.

rationale: Claim A states a block that failed checks (among other conditions) keeps its old value and stays pending. Claim B states a block that failed checks stays pending and no node is created—this is a subset of A's conditions and consequences; A's rule already covers the "failed checks → stays pending" scenario that B describes.
note: N-268's 'failed its checks' item is the same scenario N-673 describes -- correct general list / specific item relationship.

rationale: Claim A's requirement that pending blocks be processed in reproducible order subsumes Claim B's statement that blocks stay pending, since processing order presupposes blocks remain in the pending state.
note: Weak link: N-286 (processing order) doesn't really imply N-809's specific 'stays pending when the cap is hit' fact -- spurious pairing via shared 'pending' vocabulary, not a defect.

rationale: Claim A names a rule ('Check-immediately and re-ask rule'); Claim B specifies what that rule requires on failure (re-asking once with the failed check).
note: N-222 is a bullet from F3's 'In scope' list (checked the source: 'Check-immediately and re-ask rule' names a topic, it doesn't assert the rule) -- an atomization artifact, not a genuine relationship to N-241's actual rule.

rationale: Claim A specifies a selective deletion rule (delete non-best-overlapping, keep best-overlapping), which already accounts for and implies Claim B's statement that old nodes are deleted.
note: N-275 (the detailed merge mechanic: keep best-overlap, delete the rest) correctly implies N-277's simpler summary that an old node not kept is deleted.

rationale: Claim A states that F3 depends on F1 (pending blocks), which already implies that pending blocks exist and have behavior; Claim B is a specific instance of that behavior (remaining blocks stay pending).
note: N-215 is a plain dependency declaration ('F3 depends on F1'), not a substantive claim -- spurious link to N-809 via the shared phrase 'pending blocks', not a defect.

rationale: Both claims assert that removed nodes are deleted. Claim A states 'Removed nodes are deleted, not kept' and Claim B states 'Only nodes are deleted.' Both express the same fundamental requirement that nodes are deleted when removed.
note: Checked the source: N-187 is not a duplicate of N-181 at all. It's the next bullet under an explicit '⚠ Asymmetry with F1' heading, making a different point (nodes are deleted, blocks are only marked removed_run) -- and it's flagged as an open question in the text itself ('Say so if this should change too').

rationale: Both claims state the same requirement: when a node is deleted, every neighbor node that had a judged link to it gains a `stale_reasons` entry. N-000181 is the decision statement and N-000186 restates this specific consequence as an acceptance criterion.
note: Not a duplicate: N-181 is about the deleted node itself; N-186 is about its NEIGHBOURS gaining a stale_reasons flag -- different subjects. Mis-classified by the judge, but not a real issue.

rationale: Both claims state that removed/old nodes are deleted. A explicitly specifies the deletion mechanism (same transaction); B references the same requirement (citing F2 §4.9). They express the same core requirement with different levels of detail.
note: Checked the source: N-277 explicitly cites '(F2 §4.9)' rather than restating the rule -- the same deliberate cross-reference pattern as CF-000123 in Group 4, not an independent, driftable restatement.

rationale: Both claims state the same requirement: when a node is deleted, every node that had a judged link to it must gain a `stale_reasons` entry. The phrasing differs slightly but the substance is identical.
note: Checked the source: N-146 is step 4 of the deletion transaction's numbered procedure list (sec4.9); N-186 is the same fact restated under F2's separate 'what deletion costs, and how it is covered' rationale section. Mechanism + its own rationale, a deliberate documentation structure, not an independent restatement at risk of drift.

rationale: Both claims state that a lock hit replays the stored answer without making a model call, using identical core concepts.
note: Same cross-reference pattern: N-594 explicitly cites '(F3 §4.7)' rather than restating N-283's guard-rejection nuance in full.

rationale: Both claims state the same requirement: a block whose sentences are all non-normative (A) or all definition/context/rationale (B) still completes but forms nothing.
note: Checked the source: N-269 is part of F3's numbered write-procedure (item 8); N-391 is decision D33's own explanation of the same underlying fact (the I-59 finding that empty blocks were miscounted). Mechanism + decision rationale, same pattern as CF-000003.

rationale: Both claims state the same requirement: a model interface/one interface with two backends. A says 'Model interface with two backends'; B says 'Model calls go through one interface with two backends.' They describe the same structural arrangement using different terminology (model_interface = one interface; both name two backends).
note: N-220 is also a bullet from F3's 'In scope' list (same list as CF-000361's N-222; canonical modality is null, consistent with a topic name rather than a MUST-level rule) -- an atomization artifact, not a true duplicate of N-766's actual constitution-level requirement.

rationale: AC-6.8 requires that low-confidence contradicts answers create records and modify nodes immediately; N-000664 explicitly forbids filtering or re-ranking by confidence until G4 compares with human labels—these cannot both hold at the same time if AC-6.8's immediate record creation constitutes acting on confidence.
note: Same distinction as CF-000130/131 -- creating a record and adding an ambiguity flag (AC-6.8) happens the same way regardless of confidence; it isn't the filtering-or-re-ranking N-664 forbids.

rationale: Claim A specifies the node carries ambiguity `mixed_layers`, while Claim B specifies the node carries ambiguity `missing_modality`—two different ambiguities cannot both be the node's defining ambiguity state simultaneously.
note: Ambiguity is a list, not a single-value field -- a node can carry both mixed_layers (from the split-re-ask fallback, AC-3.12/D23) and missing_modality (from a null canonical.modality, F3 D14) at once, or either alone on different nodes. Not mutually exclusive.

rationale: Claim A describes conditions under which a node's status derives to ambiguous, while Claim B states that no node becomes ambiguous—both cannot hold for the same node at the same time.
note: N-368's scope is explicit in its own trigger field: 'a term verdict resolves as same' (F3 D20, Q-TERM merging). It says no node becomes ambiguous FROM a term-same merge specifically -- not a blanket denial that ambiguity (from other causes, like N-350's missing_modality) ever happens.

rationale: Claim A describes when canonical.modality is null (for a node that carries missing_modality ambiguity); Claim B requires canonical.modality to be null only in specific cases (assumption, decision, verification with no obligation). A's condition (carrying ambiguity) is not listed as a valid reason in B, creating a direct conflict.
note: A splitting artifact: N-814 and N-815 (F2 sec4.x, same block, adjacent lines) are two atoms from ONE compound sentence -- 'canonical.modality is null only for an assumption/decision/verification, OR together with ambiguity missing_modality'. The judge paired N-350 only against the first half (N-814); reading both halves together, N-350's case is exactly what the second half (N-815) permits.

rationale: AC-4.6 requires the registry to be empty when a conflict record is resolved, while AC-6.1 requires the registry to list both nodes for a conflict record, making both states impossible simultaneously.
note: Different moments in a conflict's lifecycle: AC-4.6 describes the registry after a specific conflict resolves (empty, in that isolated test); AC-6.1 describes it right after a NEW contradiction opens (lists both). Not simultaneous.

rationale: Both claims prescribe incompatible status outcomes for the same nodes when a contradicts answer is applied — one requires status conflict, the other requires ambiguity low_confidence_verdict.
note: Resolved by AC-2.12's own precedence (conflict > ambiguous > ...): a node can have both non-empty conflict_ids (from AC-6.1's contradicts verdict) and the low_confidence_verdict ambiguity entry (from AC-6.8's low-confidence case) at once -- its derived STATUS is still `conflict` either way, precedence decides which status wins, not which facts are recorded.

rationale: A requires every node's status equals F2 `derive_status` (a computed value); B requires remaining nodes keep status `unchecked` or `stale` (specific fixed values). These cannot both hold—a node cannot simultaneously have a derived status and be constrained to only `unchecked` or `stale`.
note: 'unchecked' and 'stale' are two of the five possible values derive_status can return. N-607 just names which of those values applies to nodes a stopped run didn't reach -- a specific instance of N-444's general invariant, not a competing rule.

rationale: N-000086 states placement is deterministic code over atomizer answers; N-000219 states the atomizer is the only non-deterministic component. If placement is deterministic, the atomizer cannot be the only non-deterministic component—something producing placement's inputs would also be non-deterministic.
note: A reasoning error in the rationale, not a spec conflict: a deterministic function (placement, N-086) can consume input from a non-deterministic source (the atomizer, N-219) and remain fully deterministic itself -- determinism is about the function's own behaviour, not about whether its upstream input varies.

rationale: A requires nodes with certain status conditions to be checked; B requires nodes with unchanged text/candidates to be skipped (not checked)—these are mutually exclusive requirements for the same subject.
note: Checked the source: these are the same two adjacent sentences of F5 sec4.1's node-selection rule (same block, lines 45-47) -- 'needs checking' (unchecked/stale/ambiguous-unjudged) and 'skipped, replayed from the lock' (unchanged since last check, i.e. validated) describe two non-overlapping populations, not one node in two states.

rationale: A states no node must become ambiguous; B states nodes must be checked when they are ambiguous, which presupposes nodes can become ambiguous. Both cannot hold at the same time.
note: Same narrow scope as CF-000125 -- N-368 is about term-merge outcomes only, not a claim that N-497's general ambiguous-node checking rule is vacuous.

rationale: N-000662 states confidence is 'never acted on', while N-000663 states rel01 'raises ambiguity' based on confidence—both actions on the same entity at the same time.
note: Same block (F2 B-000753), adjacent sentences of one D10 policy: 'never acted on' means confidence never changes what the compiler DOES (filter/suppress/re-rank a verdict); 'raises ambiguity' is a passive label for a human to see. Flagging is not acting on.

rationale: N-000663 describes confidence being acted on immediately by rel01 (raising ambiguity), while N-000664 prohibits any action until G4's comparison—conflicting timelines for the same entity.
note: Same distinction as CF-000130 -- raising an ambiguity flag (N-663) is not the same as filtering or re-ranking by it (N-664 forbids); the two are adjacent sentences of one coherent policy.

rationale: A requires the registry to be empty when a conflict record is resolved, while B requires the registry output to include both the registry and every open conflict record with full member records—these cannot both be true for the same conflict state.
note: N-455 says the query output always has a registry FIELD; AC-4.6 says that field's VALUE can be empty when there are no open conflicts. Always-present is compatible with sometimes-empty.

rationale: AC-3.12 states that when re-asked answer still requires split, **then the node is formed**; N-000102 states placement returns split_required and **no node is written**. Both describe the same scenario (split_required with both quotes) but reach opposite conclusions about node creation.
note: Sequential, not simultaneous: N-102 describes the FIRST placement attempt (split_required, no node written) that TRIGGERS the one re-ask; AC-3.12 describes what happens AFTER that re-ask still can't resolve it (the fallback forms a node anyway, flagged mixed_layers, per F3 D23/D36). Two stages of one pipeline.

rationale: Claim A asks to define how status and conflicts are recorded; Claim B specifies that confidence is recorded and flagged (a particular instance of recording status/conflicts), so A's broader requirement already implies B's more specific requirement.
note: Same N-082 scope-overview artifact, paired against N-662.

rationale: Claim A establishes that placement is deterministic code over atomizer answers, while Claim B specifies one particular output behavior. A's characterization subsumes the specific requirement in B.
note: N-102 (split_required, no node written) is one particular behaviour of the deterministic placement function N-086 describes generally. Correct, not a defect.

rationale: N-000444 states all nodes' status must equal derive_status; N-000350 illustrates a specific case where a node with null canonical.modality carries missing_modality ambiguity and derives to ambiguous status, which is subsumed by the general rule.
note: N-350 (a specific node's outcome: modality null + missing_modality -> ambiguous) is exactly what N-444's general invariant (status always equals derive_status) computes for those facts. Correct general/specific relationship, not a defect.

rationale: Claim A describes the concrete case where canonical.modality is null and the node carries missing_modality ambiguity and its status derives to ambiguous; Claim B is the general rule that canonical.modality MAY be together with missing_modality ambiguity, which A exemplifies.
note: N-815 is literally the rule that permits N-350's case (see CF-000268) -- correctly related, and closer to the resolving pair than a defect.

rationale: Claim A defines how status is recorded generally; Claim B specifies a particular instance where status derives to specific values (`unchecked` or `ambiguous`), which is covered by the broader claim.
note: Checked the source: N-082 is F2 sec1's own goal/scope-overview sentence ('Define the one data contract... how status and conflicts are recorded') -- a topic name, not a normative claim, so it doesn't meaningfully subsume N-524's specific rule. Atomization artifact, not a defect.

rationale: Claim A defines how status is recorded generally; Claim B specifies a particular instance where remaining nodes keep status at specific values (`unchecked` or `stale`), which is covered by the broader claim.
note: Same N-082 scope-overview artifact as CF-000237, paired against N-607 instead.

rationale: Claim A defines how status is recorded; Claim B specifies that status (along with other attributes) is computed by code, which is a particular mechanism covered by the broader requirement.
note: Same N-082 scope-overview artifact, paired against N-799.

rationale: B's requirement that every node's status equals F2 `derive_status` subsumes A's specification of when a proposed node ceases to be proposed, since the derive_status function encodes the complete status logic including the 'until confirmed' condition.
note: Same class as CF-000001 -- N-129's specific fact (a proposed node's status ends when confirmed) is consistent with, not competing with, N-444's general derive_status invariant.

rationale: AC-6.1 fully specifies that both nodes in a conflict pair carry conflict_ids and the registry lists both, which already implies N-000415's requirement that the graph keeps a registry of all conflicted nodes.
note: AC-6.1 is a testable instance of N-415's general registry feature (D9). Correct general/specific.

rationale: B states that registry and conflict records are derived and validated on every transaction; A requires these same objects to be included in query output. B's validation requirement is the broader, infrastructure-level constraint that makes A's query response possible.
note: N-465 (D2: registry and conflict records validated on every transaction) is the infrastructure guarantee that makes N-455's query-output feature trustworthy -- complementary, not competing.

rationale: Both claims state the same requirement: placement is determined by code operating on recorded answers from the atomizer. N-000086 is a more complete restatement of the same conceptual requirement expressed in N-000084.
note: N-084 is a decision-entry fragment ('decided by code from recorded answers'); N-086 is the full requirement stated right after it in the same section. A decision restating the rule it decided is the document's own structure (the same shape F6 D16/D19 suppress when a verifies-link or same-block condition is met), not an independent restatement at risk of drift.

rationale: Claim A requires F1 to provide five specific commands including `sddc add` (implicitly part of the ingest feature); Claim B explicitly withdraws `sddc add` from this spec as deferred. Both cannot hold for the same spec simultaneously.
note: The judge's own rationale is factually wrong: N-009's quoted list is 'init, ingest, status, blocks, show' -- it does not mention `sddc add` at all. N-075 (add withdrawn) doesn't contradict a list that never included it.

rationale: AC-2.19 states that when two sources carry the same human_id (`AC-1.4`), the build fails as a duplicate; N-000668 states that a local label is never adopted as a node_id and never fails a build as a duplicate. If a local label could be a source and carry `AC-1.4`, these claims directly contradict on the same scenario.
note: AC-2.19's scenario is specifically the AC-1.4-style ADOPTED id; N-668 is specifically about local labels (S1, D3-style), which by the spec's own D20 definition are never adopted and never in AC-1.4 format. The rationale's hypothetical ('if a local label could carry AC-1.4') isn't a coherent scenario in this spec's own type system.

rationale: A requires sddc commands: init, ingest, status, blocks, show; B requires: init, compile, status, conflicts, family — the command sets differ (ingest/blocks/show vs compile/conflicts/family) for the same tool.
note: N-009 is another instance of the 'In scope' list-bullet pattern (F1 sec2, same construction as N-220/N-222/N-082 found earlier) -- it names what F1's spec covers, not what ships. README.md's own text explicitly reconciles this: 'Specified but deferred out of rel01: ingest (as its own command), ..., blocks, show' -- three of N-009's five items are named there by name as specified-but-deferred.

rationale: Claim A requires sddc query command to be available, while Claim B specifies the required sddc commands for shipping as init, compile, status, conflicts, and family—omitting query from the required set.
note: Same 'in scope, not shipped' pattern as CF-000259 -- N-429 describes the query interface's design; README.md explicitly lists `query` under 'Specified but deferred out of rel01'.

rationale: Claim A explicitly withdraws fix loops as a forbidden behavior; Claim B treats fix loops as an active mechanism to be managed with deferral, creating direct opposition about the same feature's operational status.
note: N-567 and N-674 both say 'withdrawn by rel01 D26' -- they agree. N-675/N-676 are fragments of the same D8 sentence (see CF-000132) that, read whole, says the same thing N-567 does.

rationale: Claim A forbids fix loops entirely; Claim B describes fix loops as returning with live editing as an active capability, placing opposite claims about whether the same mechanism operates in the system.
note: Same as CF-000368 -- N-676 ('they return with live editing') is the second half of D8's one sentence, consistent with N-567 once read together with its own fragments.

rationale: N-000674 states the feature is 'withdrawn', while N-000675 states it is 'deferred, not deleted'—these are mutually exclusive states.
note: Checked the source: N-674/675/676 are three fragments of ONE compound sentence -- F3's D8 decision header, 'Withdrawn by rel01 D26, deferred, not deleted: [features]. They return with live editing...' The atomizer split it into three atoms and the judge compared two of its own fragments against each other. Read whole, it's one coherent statement (removed from scope now, scheduled to return later).

rationale: N-000674 states the feature is 'withdrawn', while N-000676 states 'they return'—a withdrawn feature cannot return.
note: Same three-way sentence fragmentation as CF-000132 -- N-674 and N-676 are fragments of D8's one compound sentence, not competing claims.

rationale: Claim A says the response is 'deferred, not deleted' while Claim B says it is 'return with live editing'. These are mutually exclusive outcomes for the same subject (post-edit hook trigger with AI fix loop).
note: Same three-way sentence fragmentation as CF-000132 -- the third of the three pairwise comparisons among D8's own fragments (N-675, N-676).

rationale: Claim A requires a duplicate human ID to be a build error; Claim B explicitly states a local label is 'never adopted' as a node ID and 'never fails a build as a duplicate' — these directly contradict regarding whether duplicates cause build failures.

rationale: N-000044 states timestamps appear only in runs.jsonl, while N-000440 states graph.meta.json holds no timestamps. Together these imply timestamps should appear only in runs.jsonl and nowhere else including graph.meta.json, but the claims directly contradict if timestamps exist anywhere other than runs.jsonl.
